questions.question: In a multi-agent pipeline, a downstream/receiving agent produces a wrong result because it never got the structured context it needed. Whose responsibility was that?
options: The coordinator/upstream agent's — it's responsible for passing structured context forward to the agent that needs it, not just handing off a bare task
The downstream agent's — it should have inferred the missing context on its own
It's nobody's fault, this is an expected agent failure rate
The user's, for not providing more detail in the original request

questions.question: A coordinator hands a subtask to a specialized agent but only passes a short task description, not the relevant prior findings. The specialized agent then produces an inconsistent result. Where's the root cause?
options: In the coordinator's handoff — it dropped structured context on the way down, not in the receiving agent's reasoning
In the receiving agent's tool selection
In the receiving agent's prompt engineering only
In the user's original request, since it wasn't specific enough

questions.topic: workflows vs. agents rule of thumb
questions.question: What's the rule of thumb for choosing a workflow over an agent?
options: Use a workflow when the precise series of steps is known ahead of time; use an agent when the steps aren't known and Claude needs to plan its own path with tools
Always prefer agents, since they're strictly more capable than workflows
Use a workflow only for single-step tasks and an agent for anything with more than one step
The choice depends only on which is faster to build, not on task predictability

questions.question: Claude is given a long prompt with many constraints and keeps partially ignoring some of them. Which workflow pattern actually fixes this, and why is it not routing?
options: Chaining — break the task into sequential steps and send narrow follow-up corrections; routing doesn't apply because there's nothing to classify/categorize here
Routing — classify which constraint is being violated, then forward to a specialized prompt for that constraint
Parallelization — run all the constraints as independent subtasks and aggregate
Evaluator-optimizer — since any correctness problem should default to a grader loop

questions.question: What's the parallelization workflow pattern, and what's a key benefit?
options: Split one task into independent subtasks that run concurrently, then join results in a final aggregator call — each subtask prompt stays focused, is easy to evaluate independently, and the pattern scales by adding/removing subtasks
Run the same prompt multiple times and pick the majority answer
Split a task into sequential dependent steps that must run in order
Have one Claude call classify input, then forward to a specialized downstream pipeline

questions.question: Per the course's guidance (using Claude Code as the example), how should tools given to an agent be designed?
options: Abstract and generic (e.g. bash, read, write) rather than hyper-specialized (e.g. a dedicated 'refactor' tool) — the agent combines generic tools to accomplish specific goals
As hyper-specialized as possible, one tool per exact task, to minimize ambiguity
Agents should not be given tools at all — only workflows use tools
Tools should always be paired 1:1 with each possible user request type

questions.question: Why does environment inspection matter for agents?
options: An agent needs a way to check the actual resulting state after (or before) an action, rather than just trusting what the tool call claims happened
It's only relevant for computer-use agents taking screenshots, not general-purpose agents
It replaces the need for tool descriptions entirely
It's a workflow-only concept and doesn't apply to agents

questions.question: What is the evaluator-optimizer workflow pattern?
options: A 'producer' generates output, a 'grader' checks it against criteria, and feedback loops back to the producer until the grader accepts the result
Two producers generate output independently and a human picks the better one
A single Claude call that both produces and grades its own output in one pass with no loop
Routing input to one of several specialized producers based on category

questions.question: What's the tradeoff agents make relative to workflows, per this chapter?
options: Agents trade reliability/testability for flexibility — they handle unanticipated inputs and can ask for more input, but have a lower success rate and are harder to test
Agents are strictly higher accuracy than workflows in every case
Workflows can handle unanticipated inputs better than agents
There is no meaningful tradeoff; the choice is purely stylistic

questions.question: A synthesis agent produces a report with several claims that have no source attribution. The web search and document analysis subagents are working correctly and returning well-sourced results. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The coordinator failed to forward the subagents' sourced findings as context into the synthesis agent's input
The synthesis agent's system prompt needs an explicit instruction to include citations
The web search subagent's results aren't actually well-sourced despite appearances
This is normal agent output variance and doesn't indicate an architectural issue

questions.question: A code review agent equipped with 18 tools has slow reviews and frequently selects the wrong tool. What is the most effective architectural change?
options: Split the single agent into role-scoped subagents (e.g. security, style, performance), each with a small tool subset relevant to its role
Add more detailed descriptions to all 18 tools so the single agent can distinguish them better
Reduce to a single generic tool that can perform all 18 functions via parameters
Lower the temperature so tool selection becomes more deterministic

questions.question: A coordinator agent delegates refactoring work to three specialist subagents: a schema-migration agent, an API-layer agent, and a test-update agent. The test-update agent frequently produces tests that reference database schemas the schema-migration agent has already renamed. What is the root cause?
options: The coordinator isn't forwarding the schema-migration agent's completed renames to the test-update agent before it starts writing tests
The test-update agent's prompt needs an instruction to double-check schema names before writing tests
The schema-migration agent isn't renaming things correctly
The test-update agent should be given a tool to query the database schema directly, bypassing the other subagents entirely

questions.question: A customer-support coordinator routes a ticket to a billing subagent (which confirms the customer's account tier) and then to a technical subagent (which troubleshoots a feature outage). The technical subagent's response ignores the fact that the customer's tier doesn't include that feature at all. What's the most likely root cause?
options: The coordinator never passed the billing subagent's account-tier finding into the technical subagent's input
The technical subagent's system prompt is missing an instruction to ask about account tier
The billing subagent misreported the account tier
This is expected — subagents aren't supposed to share findings with each other

questions.question: A project-planning coordinator spawns a budget subagent (which flags that the client's budget only covers 6 weeks of work) and a timeline subagent (which produces a 10-week project plan with no mention of the budget constraint). What is the most likely root cause?
options: The coordinator didn't forward the budget subagent's 6-week constraint into the timeline subagent's task input
The timeline subagent needs a tool that lets it query budget data directly
The budget subagent's estimate is probably wrong
The client's original request didn't clearly state the budget, so this is a user-input problem

questions.question: A hiring-pipeline coordinator spawns a resume-screening subagent (which rejects a candidate for missing a required certification) and an interview-scheduling subagent (which books that same candidate for an interview anyway). What is the most likely root cause?
options: The coordinator didn't pass the screening subagent's rejection verdict to the scheduling subagent before it acted
The scheduling subagent's prompt needs an explicit instruction to check certification status itself
The screening subagent evaluated the wrong certification requirement
Both subagents are working as intended — scheduling isn't supposed to depend on screening results

questions.question: A code-migration coordinator spawns a dependency-upgrade subagent (which upgrades a library from v2 to v4, noting several breaking API changes) and an integration-test subagent (which writes tests that still call the removed v2-era methods). What is the most likely root cause?
options: The coordinator didn't forward the dependency-upgrade subagent's list of breaking changes into the integration-test subagent's task
The integration-test subagent's prompt needs a rule to always check for breaking changes before writing tests
The dependency-upgrade subagent didn't actually upgrade the library correctly
The integration-test subagent should be merged into the dependency-upgrade subagent to avoid this class of bug entirely

questions.question: A multi-agent research system assigned 'renewable energy technologies' decomposes this into only 'solar panel efficiency' and 'wind turbine design.' Each subagent produces thorough, well-sourced research. The final report is comprehensive on solar and wind but missing geothermal, tidal, biomass, and nuclear fusion entirely. What is the root cause?
options: The coordinator's task decomposition was too narrow — it never assigned those subtopics to any subagent
The web search subagent failed to search broadly enough
The synthesis subagent dropped content during aggregation
The subagents didn't share memory, so coverage gaps like this are unavoidable

questions.question: For the renewable-energy coverage gap (missing geothermal, tidal, biomass, fusion), what is the correct fix?
options: Better coordinator decomposition covering the full topic breadth — not better search queries, not a stronger synthesis agent, and not more subagents
Add a more capable synthesis subagent that can catch omitted topics on its own
Improve the web search subagent's query formulation
Add more subagents to the pipeline so more ground gets covered

questions.question: A user asks a hub-and-spoke research system (with search, analysis, and synthesis subagents) a simple factual question. Per the 'dynamic subagent selection' responsibility, what should the coordinator do?
options: Dynamically select just the subagent(s) actually needed (e.g. only web search) rather than always routing through the full pipeline
Always invoke all three subagents for consistency, regardless of query complexity
Delegate to the synthesis subagent first so it can decide what other subagents are needed
Randomly select a subset of subagents to reduce load

questions.question: The coordinator delegates research on the same broad topic to two subagents. Per the 'research scope partitioning' responsibility, what should it do?
options: Assign distinct, non-overlapping subtopics or source types to each subagent (e.g. one searches academic papers, another searches news) to minimize duplication
Assign the exact same query to both subagents to cross-validate results
Let each subagent decide its own scope independently
Only use one subagent at a time so partitioning is never needed

questions.question: The coordinator evaluates its synthesis output and finds coverage gaps. Per the exam-tested 'iterative refinement' responsibility, what should happen next?
options: The coordinator re-delegates to search/analysis subagents with targeted queries addressing the gaps, then re-invokes synthesis — repeating until coverage is sufficient
The coordinator accepts the output as final, since the subagents already ran once
The synthesis subagent requests additional research directly from the search subagent
The coordinator restarts the entire pipeline from scratch with a brand-new decomposition

questions.question: An engineer proposes letting the search subagent pass results directly to the synthesis subagent, skipping a round-trip through the coordinator, to save time. Per the exam's cardinal communication rule, why is this the wrong answer even though it's more efficient?
options: Direct subagent-to-subagent communication breaks observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow — all communication must route through the coordinator regardless of efficiency gains
Subagents are technically incapable of sending messages to each other in any Claude Code implementation
It's fine as long as the coordinator is notified afterward
It's only a problem once more than two subagents are involved

questions.question: The coordinator invokes the web search subagent twice in one session — once for 'solar panel efficiency,' later for 'wind turbine costs.' What does the second invocation know about the first?
options: Nothing — every subagent invocation is completely independent; the second call has zero knowledge of the first unless the coordinator explicitly includes it in the new prompt
It automatically retains the first invocation's results in its own memory
It can look up the first invocation's results from shared global state
It inherits the coordinator's full conversation history, including the first invocation

questions.question: When the coordinator spawns a subagent, what does that subagent have access to by default?
options: Only what the coordinator explicitly includes in its prompt — not the coordinator's system prompt, prior conversation, or other subagents' results unless passed explicitly
The coordinator's full conversation history automatically
The coordinator's system prompt, but not any prior messages
Results from any other subagent already invoked in the session
